hops.title: Ball moss is not stealing from the tree
hops.text: Across the South, gray-green clumps about the size of baseballs hang from tree branches, and people often blame them for the dead limbs they sit on. Ball moss is not a true moss or a parasite. It is a cousin of the pineapple, and its short anchors only grip; they take no water or food from the tree. The proof: the same plant grows on bare telephone wires, fences and even traffic lights. With no soil in reach, it builds its body from carbon dioxide, water and a little dust.

sources.citation: Raghuwinder Singh, Louisiana Plant Health Management: Ball Moss (Tillandsia recurvata), LSU AgCenter Publication 4023.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Round gray-green clumps of ball moss sitting along a bare overhead wire against a blue sky, with a small bird on the wire looking at one clump.
image.caption: Ball moss lives on bare wires, building its body mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, plus water.

hops.title: Why space lettuce can look the wrong color
hops.text: On the International Space Station, astronauts grow red romaine lettuce in Veggie, a garden about the size of a carry-on bag. Its lights are mostly red and blue, the colors chlorophyll absorbs well, so the box glows magenta pink. Why add a few green LEDs at all? Under red and blue alone, plants look purplish-gray, and a sick leaf is hard to spot. The green lights are there for the astronauts' eyes, so the lettuce looks like food instead of strange purple leaves.

sources.citation: Mickens, Massa, Newsham, Wheeler and Birmele (2016), Comparative Study of Lettuce and Radish Grown Under Red and Blue LEDs and White Fluorescent Lamps, NASA Technical Reports Server 20160006559.
NASA, Spinoff and Mission Updates newsletter, September 2015, "Lettuce Eat" (Veggie LED lights).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An astronaut seen from behind peering into a small magenta-lit plant box on a space station that holds six lettuce plants.
image.caption: Chlorophyll captures red and blue light well; a little green light helps astronauts spot sick leaves.

hops.title: Greenhouses that run low on carbon dioxide
hops.text: A sealed glass greenhouse on a bright day looks like plant heaven. But outside air holds about 400 parts per million of carbon dioxide, and busy crops can pull the air inside down to 150 to 200. Then extra sunshine helps less, because carbon dioxide has become the limit. Growers add it from tanks or burners, aiming for about 1,000 parts per million. By one estimate, most crops then photosynthesize up to half again as fast. Workers breathing in the aisles chip in a little too.

sources.citation: Bruce Dunn and Megha Poudel (2023), Greenhouse Carbon Dioxide Supplementation, Oklahoma State University Extension HLA-6723.
Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, "Supplemental carbon dioxide in greenhouses."

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Rows of tall tomato plants with red fruit inside a sunny glass greenhouse, a thin pipe along the base of each row and a worker seen from behind walking down the aisle.
image.caption: In a closed greenhouse, carbon dioxide can run low, and then brighter sunlight barely speeds up the crops.

audio.title: Hidden ocean cells, stolen chloroplasts and sleeping with plants
audio.transcript:
When you hear the word photosynthesis, you probably picture an oak tree or a fern on a windowsill. Fair enough. Trees are great at it. But some of the strangest photosynthesis on Earth happens in places you would never think to look. And it clears up an old bedtime rumor along the way.

Start in the open ocean. The most abundant photosynthetic cell on the whole planet hid in plain sight until nineteen eighty-eight. That year, the oceanographer Penny Chisholm and her colleagues announced a tiny marine cyanobacterium that they later named Prochlorococcus. It is a prokaryote, so it has no chloroplasts at all. Each cell is roughly one millionth of a meter across. What gave it away was a red glow, a chlorophyll signal, picked up in ocean water samples. Once scientists knew how to look, they estimated that the oceans hold about three billion billion billion of these cells. Powered by sunlight, they pull carbon out of carbon dioxide and build it into living cells. By one estimate, the carbon they lock into new cells each year weighs about four billion tons, as much as five billion old Volkswagen Beetles. That is about eight and a half percent of all the photosynthesis in the ocean. Not bad for a cell you could mistake for a speck of dust.

Now jump from a cell with no chloroplasts to an animal that borrows them. In shallow coastal water lives a sea slug called Elysia chlorotica. Animals cannot make chloroplasts, so this slug takes them. It eats an alga called Vaucheria litorea and tucks the alga's chloroplasts, still whole, inside its own cells. The alga's nucleus is gone, yet those borrowed chloroplasts keep working for several months. They take in carbon dioxide, release oxygen and even build proteins. So the slug may get some of its food from sunlight. Scientists are still working out how the chloroplasts keep going without their old nucleus, and how much the slug really depends on them.

Finally, bring all of this back to your bedroom. You may have heard the warning never to sleep with houseplants in your room, because at night they give off carbon dioxide and steal your oxygen. Here is the funny part: the biology behind that rumor is half true. Plant cells carry out cellular respiration twenty-four hours a day, breaking down the sugar made in photosynthesis and giving off carbon dioxide. During the day in good light, photosynthesis usually runs faster than respiration, so the plant gives off oxygen overall. At night, with no light, photosynthesis stops while respiration keeps ticking along. So why can the fern stay beside your bed? Because over one night, a houseplant uses only a tiny fraction of the oxygen already in the room. You will wake up breathing just fine.

An invisible ocean cell, a slug with stolen chloroplasts and a fern on your dresser. Photosynthesis is quietly running the planet, and it does not stop for bedtime rumors.
